content: Köhler disease, also known as Köhler first disease or osteochondrosis of the tarsal navicular, is a rare bone disorder affecting the foot in children, typically between the ages of six and nine. This condition was first described in 1908 by Alban Köhler, a German radiologist. The disease occurs when the navicular bone in the foot temporarily loses its blood supply, leading to bone tissue death and subsequent collapse of the bone. However, with appropriate treatment, the condition does not result in long-term complications. As the navicular bone heals and returns to its normal state, symptoms usually resolve. The exact cause of Köhler disease remains unknown, but it is thought to result from excessive strain on a structurally weak navicular bone. Patients with Köhler disease often present with pain and swelling in the midfoot region, which may cause them to limp. While the condition is more commonly observed in boys, it can also affect girls. Boys around the age of five are most frequently affected, and patients often report localized pain over the apex of the navicular bone. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through X-ray imaging of both feet. The affected foot will show a dense, flattened navicular bone on the X-ray. Treatment often involves immobilizing the affected foot with a cast that extends below the knee. Moderate physical activity is generally encouraged, as it can aid in recovery.
